title: Why Rejoin UNIDO? UK Officials Make the Case
label: 15 Sep 2026 · UNIDO evidence
summary: The International Agreements Committee questioned Matt Toombs and Paul Durrant from the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero about why the UK should rejoin UNIDO, the United Nations Industrial Development Organization. The witnesses argued that the context has changed since the UK left in 2012, that UNIDO has reformed and become more efficient and transparent, and that the UK already works closely with it on green industrial projects. They faced tough questions about whether rejoining delivers value for money, helps the poorest countries access climate finance, coordinates with other countries, and avoids slipping back into old problems. Toombs said the UK will review the benefits of rejoining in 2029.

speakers.label: Matt Toombs
speakers.name: Matt Toombs
speakers.role: Director for International Net Zero - Climate Finance and Strategy, Department for Energy Security and Net Zero

speakers.label: Paul Durrant
speakers.name: Paul Durrant
speakers.role: Head of the International Green Industrialisation, Technology Innovation & Electrification (IGNITE) team, Department for Energy Security and Net Zero

chapters.title: The case for rejoining
chapters.takeaway: The UK left UNIDO in 2012, but the government says the world has changed and UNIDO has reformed, so rejoining now makes sense.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We've just heard from UNIDO staff. The big question is: why should we rejoin? We already have a good relationship with them, and we don't need to get involved in their politics. Also, what genuine reforms have been made that justify reversing our decision to leave 15 years ago? That decision was carefully made, so we need convincing.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Thank you. The context now is very different from 2012, and our relationship with UNIDO has changed too. Over the past five years we've worked with them on many programmes. Clean, green industrial development is critical for developing countries' economies. The question is how to make it sustainable and how the UK can benefit from the growth.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: In 2012 we had almost no programmes with UNIDO. Since then we've worked together on things like COP 26, green public procurement with India, and the Accelerate-to-Demonstrate programme, which is about £125 million. We've also worked with Brazil on industrial decarbonisation. So the relationship is much deeper, and rejoining would give us more influence and open doors for British business.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: On reforms: UNIDO is smaller and more efficient than when we left. It's more transparent, publishes information about its programmes, and has an independent evaluation unit. That's why we think it's worth re-engaging.

chapters.title: What other countries are doing
chapters.takeaway: Many industrialised countries stayed in UNIDO, and some that left may rejoin, but the UK won't speak for them.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anelay of St Johns
turns.text: You say the context has changed. What about other countries that left? Have you talked to them about returning? If they're not, why not, given the benefits you mention?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: We're in conversation with like-minded countries, but I won't speak for them. Many industrialised countries like Japan, Italy, Germany and the EU remain in UNIDO. We wouldn't be an exception. We've been building this relationship for at least five years.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anelay of St Johns
turns.text: Some countries still think it's not worth joining. Do you think others might rejoin?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Yes, short answer. Next week at the UN General Assembly and Climate Week NYC there will be discussions on green industrialisation. It matters a lot to developing countries and to the Turkish and Ethiopian COP presidencies. Other countries may take a similar route to us.

chapters.title: Does it help the poorest?
chapters.takeaway: Toombs argues that UNIDO membership helps scale up climate finance and deliver practical benefits, but Lord Boateng presses him on water and sanitation.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: Countries like Japan, Italy and Germany have always believed in industrial policy and their economies thrived. But we've spent billions on aid with insufficient impact. Now our development budget is cut. Why should we pay a subscription to UNIDO when that money could go to projects? I chair Water & Sanitation for Urban Populations. How will UNIDO membership help people facing climate and water emergencies, especially when less than 3% of global climate finance goes to water and sanitation? Girls miss school because they lack decent toilets. How does UNIDO help the most marginalised?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: I agree we need climate finance to reach those who need it most. Our international climate finance is smaller now, so we have to prioritise. The government's 2026 strategy says we need that money to go further and mobilise larger amounts.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: That's good, but how does UNIDO membership specifically assist people who can't access the Green Climate Fund?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: By being a member, we can help scale up solutions rather than just small projects. For example, in Brazil about £15 million of UK investment helped unlock £250 million of wider international finance, expected to raise £2 billion in private finance. That changes livelihoods and creates jobs.

chapters.title: Making finance easier to access
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses agree climate finance is too hard to access and that foreign aid rules need rethinking, but private sector involvement is essential.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: Is it time to revisit how climate finance is accessed? People on the ground say it's complicated, slow and full of hurdles. Also, is our overseas aid system fit for this century?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: I agree access is a challenge. The UK works with the Green Climate Fund to speed up access. It's a wider issue, not specific to UNIDO. With smaller aid budgets, we need to use money where it can have the greatest impact and mobilise other sources.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: Are you restricted in how you spend aid with private companies? To get private investment, aid needs to be easier for businesses to navigate.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Absolutely. Private sector involvement is critical. We have examples with UK businesses working with Kenya on green tea and South Africa on green steel. We won't make progress without the private sector fully involved.

chapters.title: Engagement with other countries
chapters.takeaway: The UK talks to Australia and others about industrial development, but won't comment on whether they will rejoin UNIDO.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: What about the US, Australia and New Zealand? Have you engaged with them? Are they likely to go back?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: I won't speak for individual countries. The US position on climate change is well known, and it has withdrawn from several agencies. We work with Australia and New Zealand closely. Australia is co-president of this year's COP with Turkey, so we discuss industrial development with them.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: Do you know if Australia is going back?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: I wouldn't want to comment on their specific relationship with UNIDO.

chapters.title: Will UNIDO stay on track?
chapters.takeaway: The UK plans to review the benefits of rejoining in 2029, and membership gives the UK more leverage to keep UNIDO reforming.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: I was British ambassador to the UN in the 1990s. We're told UNIDO is reforming, but how do we ensure it doesn't slip back, like the FAO did? And how do we stop UN agencies turf-fighting with each other?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: We wouldn't assume things won't slip back. Being a member gives us more oversight and stronger levers. The UN80 reform process is streamlining agencies. And we have a plan to review whether we're achieving the benefits of rejoining in 2029.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: So that review would decide whether we sustain membership or withdraw again?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Our intention is to make this a positive, sustained relationship. But it's right to review in three years.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: If Parliament is involved in that review, would it help your hand in UNIDO governance?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: The review point is for the UK to decide, not part of a formal agreement with UNIDO.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: So it's a UK review of our decision, not a UNIDO review.
